_meta.about: Burmeister's self-help material as the site shows it, read by site/src/data/selfhelp.ts. Everything here is paraphrase checked against the printed books on 2026-10-31. `ref` keeps the page for the audit trail; the page does not show it. The books stay in research/books and are not reproduced.

items.d: Sit, stand or lie down, wherever it is easiest.
Stay dressed. A hold works through clothes, and even through a cast.
Palm, thumb tip, fingers or the back of the hand: whichever is comfortable.
Rest the hand. It takes no great pressure, and no rubbing or massage.
Until you feel a steady pulse, or at first a few minutes a step. With four steps and fifteen minutes, three or four minutes each.
Only the tenser side needs the sequence. Until you can tell, do both; the easier side settles sooner.
Skip it. There are no set rules, and each sequence can be fitted to you.
Burmeister’s measure is at least half an hour to an hour a day.
Not your own. She says the hands draw on a universal supply, not on anything within us.
She calls this an art and not a technique: you are the artist, and the sequences are yours to fit. Be your own testimony, she says.

steps: Let the head bow until it feels weightless.
Breathe out first, unloading from head to toes.
Breathe in, receiving from toes to head.
breath.note: She gives this with the palm centres held. She names the same 36 breaths with the hands folded, or the fingers held in turn.

projects.d: The six steps of the Main Central and the three steps, each side, of the Supervisor and Mediator. A warm-up in the morning, a clean-up at night. Either set alone will do.
Notice which attitude is strongest right now and do its short finger sequence, or just hold its one finger: thumb for worry, index for fear, middle for anger, ring for grief, little for pretence.
Three daily sequences, later called the Spleen, Stomach and Bladder flows.
Short holds for wherever they are needed.

shortHolds.d: Thumb on the inner upper arm, fingers on the outer.
Palms or backs under the sitting bones.
Sit on one hand and lay the other over the shoulder on that side.
shortHolds.for: That side of the abdomen, overeating, breathing

shortHolds.d: Arms crossed, each palm on the opposite thigh. One will do if the other hand is busy.
Fingers or thumbs on the upper calves, just under the crease.
Thumbs on the front of the shoulder joints, fingers by the shoulder blades.

items.d: Right hand on the place, left hand over it. Traditionally for bleeding and hernia-like troubles.
Left hand on the place, right hand over it. Traditionally for a splinter, or to bring a pimple to a head.
Rest a palm on a minor burn or a grazed knee.

palming.direction: Book 3 also gives the current’s direction in the limbs: with the arms raised, as she draws it, the current in the right arm and leg rises up the back and falls down the front; on the left, the reverse.

fingerNotesRef: aids SH1 p.55 and SH3 pp.27-39, keeping only her lettered statements and leaving out the first-person complaint lists; toes SH3 pp.26-40 (opposite printed for thumb and little toe, p.29, and index and little toe, p.3; the rest follows pp.18-19); order of creation SH3 p.28

points.t: Back of the hand, sole of the foot
points.d: The back of one hand answers to the opposite sole, and the palm to the top of the opposite foot.

The top third of a finger, toe, palm or sole relates to mind and feeling, the brain, chest and thighs; the middle third to digestion, the face, abdomen and calves; the bottom third to the body, the neck, pelvis and feet. On the palm and sole, every third also touches the brain, bar the top third, where it is already named.

points.t: Centre of the palm and sole
points.d: Both stand for the Main Central and balance the whole body. Book 3 also puts the source of energy for every cell in the palms and soles. To hold a sole, clamp the foot with the hand of the same side, fingers on the centre of the sole and thumb on top.
It can stand in for the thumb, one elbow at a time or both.
Hold the finger, its toe, or both. The one in need is whichever feels easiest, or sorest, to hold.
Book 3 says to go to the finger as a complaint begins: the thumb for a headache, the little finger for a sore throat, the index for a backache.
Fingers and palms, toes and soles all work on the Main Central, and through it on the organs and glands.

fingersToes.conflict: Book 3 pairs the little toe two ways. Its opening example joins the index finger to the opposite little toe for back tension (p.3), while its fuller pages join index to ring toe and thumb to little toe (pp.29-31). The atlas follows the fuller pages.

mudras.intro: These are Murai’s own poses, the ones he used in his illness. Book 3 calls them finger poses; mudra is the usual word elsewhere. Use them whenever you like and for as long as you like; there’s no need to do all eight at one sitting. Burmeister suggests two breaths in each pose, then folding the hands for the rest of a count of 36.

items.how: Thumb on the palm side of the other hand’s middle finger, fingers on its back.
items.for: Releases from head to toe, with the out-breath

items.how: Thumb on the back of the other hand’s middle finger, fingers on its palm side.
items.for: Revitalises from toes to head, with the in-breath

items.how: Thumb on the palm side of the other hand’s little and ring fingers, fingers on their back.
Thumb on the back of the other hand’s thumb, index and middle fingers, fingers on their palm side.
Ring the right thumb and middle finger, thumb on the nail. Pass the left thumb through the ring to rest on that same nail. Swap hands for the other side.
Rest the pad of the thumb on the ring fingernail of the same hand, on either hand.
items.for: Breathing, ears; useful walking, exercising or at altitude

items.how: Fold the hands with the palm sides of the two middle fingers touching.
items.for: Head, lungs, digestion, abdomen, legs, with the out-breath

items.how: Bring the two middle fingernails together.
items.for: Back, whole body, with the in-breath
